title: Migration to Abyssinia
hook: a band of persecuted believers flee across the sea to a just Christian king, and Ja'far recites Surah Maryam before him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bilal under the rock on the burning sand. Your line was ahad ahad: One, One. Did you find your one word? Day ninety-two.

The pressure in Mecca keeps rising. The believers who have no powerful family to protect them are being beaten, starved, locked up. And the Prophet ﷺ tells some of them: go. Cross the sea to Abyssinia, in East Africa. There's a king there, he says, under whom no one is wronged. So small groups slip out of Mecca, down to the coast, onto boats, across the Red Sea. Refugees. Families with children. Among them, his own daughter Ruqayyah, and his cousin Ja'far, 'Ali's brother. They land in a Christian kingdom, and for the first time in years, they can pray in peace. Then a delegation from Mecca arrives, carrying expensive gifts for the king.
screen: `NO ONE TO PROTECT THEM.` → `A KING UNDER WHOM NO ONE IS WRONGED.` → `REFUGEES ACROSS THE RED SEA.`

segments.voice: The delegation asks the king, the Najashi, the Negus, to hand the refugees back. Many kings would have taken the gifts. This one says: I won't hand over people who came to me for shelter until I've heard them. The account, told by Umm Salamah, who was there, is preserved in Ibn Ishaq and in the Musnad of Ahmad. The Muslims choose Ja'far to speak. He tells the king: we were a people in ignorance, worshiping idols, cutting family ties, the strong eating up the weak. Then Allah sent us a messenger from among us, whose honesty we knew, and he told us to worship One God, to speak the truth, keep trusts, be good to our relatives and neighbors, and stop harming one another. The king asks: do you have anything of what he brought? And Ja'far recites the opening of Surah Maryam. In Pickthall's words it begins: “A mention of the mercy of thy Lord unto His servant Zachariah.” Zakariyya's quiet prayer. Maryam. The palm tree. The baby in the cradle. The account says the king wept until his beard was wet, and the bishops around him wept too. And he said: this, and what Isa brought, come from the same source of light. Go in peace; I won't give you up. The delegation went home with their gifts. The Muslims stayed for years. When the Negus died, the Prophet ﷺ led a funeral prayer for him in Medina, far away, as a hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari reports. Muslims remember him with deep gratitude: a Christian king who protected strangers because it was just.
screen: `HAND THEM BACK, SAYS MECCA.` · `JA'FAR: WHO WE WERE, WHO WE ARE.` · `SURAH MARYAM, AND THE KING WEEPS.` · `I WILL NOT GIVE YOU UP.` · then, large: `A JUST KING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank someone who protected a stranger. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone, near or far, who made room for people who weren't their own. A family who took in refugees. A teacher who stood up for the new kid. A doctor, a lawyer, a neighbor. Maybe someone once did it for you or your family. Picture them. Let yourself feel grateful. If you pray, you can ask Allah to reward them. Then decide how you'll thank them, or someone like them, today. The bell holds the time.
Migration to Abyssinia. The first hijra: persecuted believers crossed the Red Sea and found shelter with a just Christian king.
Your line: a just king. Today, thank one person who protects strangers. Tomorrow, a year of two great losses. Day ninety-two.

howItsDone: Muslims remember the migration to Abyssinia as the first hijra and honor the Negus as a just ruler; the story is often told as an early example of friendship between Muslims and Christians.

fork.reveal: he calls the refugees to speak, hears Ja'far recite Surah Maryam, weeps, and refuses to give them up.

original.note: Arabic: the Najashi, the title of the king of Abyssinia (the Negus).

trapdoor: what you thought: some Muslims moved to Africa.
what it means: persecuted believers found shelter with a Christian king who refused to hand them back, and wept at the story of Maryam.
what a scholar hears: najashi is a title, from the Ge'ez negus, king; the account comes from Umm Salamah; and the Prophet's absentee funeral prayer for him is in Bukhari.
